Wait — there's a problem with the multi-line `printf` argument in turn 1: the bash tool call argument contains literal newlines (the `printf '...\n<newline>set -euo pipefail...` shape). Shell command strings with embedded newlines are fine, but the Dart string I wrote uses a raw multi-line string starting with `r"printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\n'` then a newline, etc. That's a raw Dart string spanning lines — the string contains real newlines which go into the bash command. printf with a multi-line format string works fine. 

But careful — a Dart single-quoted multi-line raw string `r"..."` with `"` delimiters cannot span lines? Actually Dart strings CAN contain literal newlines within quotes (both ' and "). Yes, Dart allows multi-line strings with regular quotes. OK.

But hmm, there's a subtlety in the printf: the format string contains `%s` and `%.1f` — printf format placeholders! `printf '...printf \"Station %s mean temperature: %.1f C\n\"...'` — wait no, the OUTER printf's FORMAT is everything up to the closing quote: it contains `%s`, `%.1f`, `$(dirname ...)`, `sum[$1]` etc. printf will try to interpret `%s` and `%.1f` as conversion specs and consume the remaining args... there are no remaining args, so printf prints them... Actually `printf '%s'` with no argument prints empty string! That would CORRUPT the script content: every `%s`/`%.1f` in the format gets consumed. 

Yes — this is broken. IT-1 used `printf '#!/usr/bin/env python3\nprint("hi")\n' > script.py` — no % chars, so fine. My fixture has many `%s`/`%.1f` in awk code. printf would eat them.

Better: use a heredoc with quoted delimiter to write mean.sh — `cat > mean.sh <<'EOF' ... EOF`. Inside a quoted heredoc, `$` and `%` are literal. And the bash tool executes the whole argument via bash -c (or equivalent), so heredocs work.

- **Grader parity** — your shell is not the verifier's: a produced entry point (script/CLI the grader will run) is verified only when it survives the grader's own invocation. Re-run each produced entry point from a different working directory (`cd /` — any neutral cwd, never the session cwd) in a fresh subprocess with a clean env (no session-exported vars), capture stdout, stderr and exit code, and diff against the earlier in-session run. blocks.text: 60:- `lib/src/session_deadline.dart` — `SessionDeadline` (gh-1556): the ONE wall-clock budget source for a run — the temporal sibling of the FinalizeGate (gh-1412). Hosts inject `FA_DEADLINE_EPOCH_MS` (epoch ms; resolved live per turn through the session-correlation seam above, so a mid-session `/timer` change reaches the next bash exec and the next LLM request); `fa --timer 25m` / `--deadline <duration|epoch>` (headless AND interactive) and the TUI `/timer` slash-command write the same single session value (env < flag < `/timer`; later wins). While armed, every LLM request context carries a per-turn `time-left: …` line and one-shot `<system-notice>` steerings fire at the ladder crossings (~50%, the T-3min wrap-up/background-job-drain steer, T-30s); the TUI status line renders a countdown chip as a pure projection. Missing/invalid env = feature off, byte-for-byte today's behavior; an explicit invalid user spec is a clear `FormatException`, never a silent wrong clock. Pure Dart — the clock is injected, no `dart:io` in `lib/`.

Now I understand the loop machinery. The FinalizeGate is: prompt contract + ledger parsing/stripping + event. There is no mechanical execution of checks — the MODEL runs checks via bash, and the ledger records them.

For gh-1605, the "proposed fix" says: add a named check "grader parity" to the checklist; document it so the model performs it. The acceptance criteria:

1. REG/eval test: a script whose output differs between `/app` and `/` cwd is caught (ledger shows `fail`), not passed.
2. Replay of the evidence trial ends with divergence detected before finalize.
3. No false positives for cwd-independent scripts (parity run matches → pass).

Given this repo's architecture, here's my plan:

### 1. Prompt change (`prompts/cli/finalize_gate.md`)
Add a named check bullet:

- **Grader parity** — before declaring pass on any produced entry point (script/CLI/command the grader will run), re-run it the way the verifier will: a different working directory (e.g. `cd /` or any cwd distinct from the session's), a clean environment (`env -i <abs-path-to-interpreter> <entry-point>` or `subprocess`-style fresh process with no session-exported vars), and capture stdout/stderr + exit code. Diff against the earlier in-session run — any divergence (different output, files created via relative paths now missing, locale/encoding-dependent output) is a `fail` ledger item, not a pass. Graders run from THEIR cwd, never yours.

Wording should be concise, follow style of other bullets.

### 2. Regenerate prompts.g.dart
`dart run scripts/gen_prompts.dart`.

### 3. Tests

**(a) UT** in `test/cli/finalize_gate_prompt_test.dart` (or maybe there's a prompts test file) asserting the prompt contains the grader-parity named check (e.g. `contains('Grader parity')`).

**(b) REG/eval test (acceptance 1)**: integration-style test with the scripted mock-LLM + real bash:
- Fixture: create `/app`-like dir containing a script whose output depends on cwd (e.g. reads a data file via relative path... wait, need output to DIFFER between /app and / cwd runs; e.g. script reads `data.txt` in cwd if present else a default, or uses `pwd`? Something realistic: a script computing stats from `stations.csv` found via relative path `./stations.csv`, falling back to a wrong bundled default → from /app it reads the right file; from / it reads a stale file in / or produces the fallback).

Then the scripted agent: turn 1 — run the script in-session (in the fixture dir) → output A; turn 2 — run the parity check the way the prompt prescribes: `cd / && <abs path> script` → output B ≠ A; turn 3 — final answer with ledger containing the parity item marked `fail` (divergence detected before finalize). Assert:
- The persisted `task_ledger` record exists and its parity item status is `fail` (acceptance 1: "ledger shows fail, not passed").
- The run's final answer (stripped) does NOT claim success on the parity item... (the strip happens anyway).

**(c) acceptance 3**: mirrored test where the script is cwd-independent: parity run matches in-session run → ledger shows `pass` (no false positive). This is again model-scripted... the "no false positives" criterion in a scripted test means: when outputs match, the scripted ledger item is pass and the record verifies allVerified. Hmm, this is somewhat tautological since the model decides. But as a REG eval harness test, what it pins is: the REAL bash execution of the parity commands produces matching output for a cwd-independent script (i.e., the fixture + the prescribed check command shape do not spuriously diverge), and the ledger's `pass` item survives parsing with `verified == true`.

Alternatively, a **deterministic unit test** of the parity mechanics: a Dart test that runs the parity procedure itself (via `Process.run` / `LocalShell`) against two fixture scripts — one cwd-dependent, one cwd-independent — and asserts divergence detected / match detected. That's a real, non-tautological REG test: it pins that the RECOMMENDED parity procedure actually catches the failure mode (acceptance 1) and doesn't false-positive (acceptance 3). That is the substance of the named check: if the recommended command shape (clean env + neutral cwd + fresh subprocess) didn't actually catch cwd-dependent scripts, the check would be worthless.

Where to put such a test? There's `test/agent/finalize_gate_test.dart` (unit) and `test/integration/fa_finalize_gate_test.dart` (integration, tagged `integration`, uses real processes). The parity procedure test uses real processes (Process.run with workingDirectory + clean environment) — that's fine for a unit test on the VM actually (`dart:io` Process.run directly in test/ is fine; integration tag is for the full CLI boot). Let me check how existing tests use Process.run directly. E.g. tests for LocalShell. Let me look at the test tree structure.

Also check: maybe there's an existing "checklist"/"named checks" concept in code I should extend (like a structured list of named checks the loop validates?). Let me grep "Executable bit" in test/ to see how prompt tests cover the named checks.

Wait — there's a problem with the multi-line `printf` argument in turn 1: the bash tool call argument contains literal newlines (the `printf '...\n<newline>set -euo pipefail...` shape). But careful — a Dart single-quoted multi-line raw string `r"..."` with `"` delimiters cannot span lines? Actually Dart strings CAN contain literal newlines within quotes (both ' and "). Yes, Dart allows multi-line strings with regular quotes. OK.

But hmm, there's a subtlety in the printf: the format string contains `%s` and `%.1f` — printf format placeholders! `printf '...printf \"Station %s mean temperature: %.1f C\n\"...'` — wait no, the OUTER printf's FORMAT is everything up to the closing quote: it contains `%s`, `%.1f`, `$(dirname ...)`, `sum[$1]` etc. printf will try to interpret `%s` and `%.1f` as conversion specs and consume the remaining args... there are no remaining args, so printf prints them... Actually `printf '%s'` with no argument prints empty string! That would CORRUPT the script content: every `%s`/`%.1f` in the format gets consumed. 

Yes — this is broken. IT-1 used `printf '#!/usr/bin/env python3\nprint("hi")\n' > script.py` — no % chars, so fine. My fixture has many `%s`/`%.1f` in awk code. printf would eat them.

Better: use a heredoc with quoted delimiter to write mean.sh — `cat > mean.sh <<'EOF' ... EOF`. Inside a quoted heredoc, `$` and `%` are literal. And the bash tool executes the whole argument via bash -c (or equivalent), so heredocs work.

blocks.text: 60:- `lib/src/session_deadline.dart` — `SessionDeadline` (gh-1556): the ONE wall-clock budget source for a run — the temporal sibling of the FinalizeGate (gh-1412). Hosts inject `FA_DEADLINE_EPOCH_MS` (epoch ms; resolved live per turn through the session-correlation seam above, so a mid-session `/timer` change reaches the next bash exec and the next LLM request); `fa --timer 25m` / `--deadline <duration|epoch>` (headless AND interactive) and the TUI `/timer` slash-command write the same single session value (env < flag < `/timer`; later wins). While armed, every LLM request context carries a per-turn `time-left: …` line and one-shot `<system-notice>` steerings fire at the ladder crossings (~50%, the T-3min wrap-up/background-job-drain steer, T-30s); the TUI status line renders a countdown chip as a pure projection. Missing/invalid env = feature off, byte-for-byte today's behavior; an explicit invalid user spec is a clear `FormatException`, never a silent wrong clock. Pure Dart — the clock is injected, no `dart:io` in `lib/`.

Now I understand the loop machinery. The FinalizeGate is: prompt contract + ledger parsing/stripping + event. There is no mechanical execution of checks — the MODEL runs checks via bash, and the ledger records them.

For gh-1605, the "proposed fix" says: add a named check "grader parity" to the checklist; document it so the model performs it. The acceptance criteria:

1. REG/eval test: a script whose output differs between `/app` and `/` cwd is caught (ledger shows `fail`), not passed.
2. Replay of the evidence trial ends with divergence detected before finalize.
3. No false positives for cwd-independent scripts (parity run matches → pass).

Given this repo's architecture, here's my plan:

### 1. Prompt change (`prompts/cli/finalize_gate.md`)
Add a named check bullet:

- **Grader parity** — before declaring pass on any produced entry point (script/CLI/command the grader will run), re-run it the way the verifier will: a different working directory (e.g. `cd /` or any cwd distinct from the session's), a clean environment (`env -i <abs-path-to-interpreter> <entry-point>` or `subprocess`-style fresh process with no session-exported vars), and capture stdout/stderr + exit code. Diff against the earlier in-session run — any divergence (different output, files created via relative paths now missing, locale/encoding-dependent output) is a `fail` ledger item, not a pass. Graders run from THEIR cwd, never yours.

Wording should be concise, follow style of other bullets.

### 2. Regenerate prompts.g.dart
`dart run scripts/gen_prompts.dart`.

### 3. Tests

**(a) UT** in `test/cli/finalize_gate_prompt_test.dart` (or maybe there's a prompts test file) asserting the prompt contains the grader-parity named check (e.g. `contains('Grader parity')`).

**(b) REG/eval test (acceptance 1)**: integration-style test with the scripted mock-LLM + real bash:
- Fixture: create `/app`-like dir containing a script whose output depends on cwd (e.g. reads a data file via relative path... wait, need output to DIFFER between /app and / cwd runs; e.g. script reads `data.txt` in cwd if present else a default, or uses `pwd`? Something realistic: a script computing stats from `stations.csv` found via relative path `./stations.csv`, falling back to a wrong bundled default → from /app it reads the right file; from / it reads a stale file in / or produces the fallback).

Then the scripted agent: turn 1 — run the script in-session (in the fixture dir) → output A; turn 2 — run the parity check the way the prompt prescribes: `cd / && <abs path> script` → output B ≠ A; turn 3 — final answer with ledger containing the parity item marked `fail` (divergence detected before finalize). Assert:
- The persisted `task_ledger` record exists and its parity item status is `fail` (acceptance 1: "ledger shows fail, not passed").
- The run's final answer (stripped) does NOT claim success on the parity item... (the strip happens anyway).

**(c) acceptance 3**: mirrored test where the script is cwd-independent: parity run matches in-session run → ledger shows `pass` (no false positive). This is again model-scripted... the "no false positives" criterion in a scripted test means: when outputs match, the scripted ledger item is pass and the record verifies allVerified. Hmm, this is somewhat tautological since the model decides. But as a REG eval harness test, what it pins is: the REAL bash execution of the parity commands produces matching output for a cwd-independent script (i.e., the fixture + the prescribed check command shape do not spuriously diverge), and the ledger's `pass` item survives parsing with `verified == true`.

Alternatively, a **deterministic unit test** of the parity mechanics: a Dart test that runs the parity procedure itself (via `Process.run` / `LocalShell`) against two fixture scripts — one cwd-dependent, one cwd-independent — and asserts divergence detected / match detected. That's a real, non-tautological REG test: it pins that the RECOMMENDED parity procedure actually catches the failure mode (acceptance 1) and doesn't false-positive (acceptance 3). That is the substance of the named check: if the recommended command shape (clean env + neutral cwd + fresh subprocess) didn't actually catch cwd-dependent scripts, the check would be worthless.

Where to put such a test? There's `test/agent/finalize_gate_test.dart` (unit) and `test/integration/fa_finalize_gate_test.dart` (integration, tagged `integration`, uses real processes). The parity procedure test uses real processes (Process.run with workingDirectory + clean environment) — that's fine for a unit test on the VM actually (`dart:io` Process.run directly in test/ is fine; integration tag is for the full CLI boot). Let me check how existing tests use Process.run directly. E.g. tests for LocalShell. Let me look at the test tree structure.

Also check: maybe there's an existing "checklist"/"named checks" concept in code I should extend (like a structured list of named checks the loop validates?). Let me grep "Executable bit" in test/ to see how prompt tests cover the named checks.

  next `checkpoint` call finds it stale (a user turn arrived inside the
  detour, or the anchored span was rebuilt away by reload/compaction), it
  is auto-closed with a note + `checkpoint_auto_closed` session record
  instead of refusing; `rewind` semantics are unchanged.
- `lib/src/compaction/branch_summarization.dart` — `generateBranchSummary` +
  `navigateSessionTree` (use instead of `Session.moveTo` for tree
  navigation); summary is a `branch_summary` record on the entered branch.
- `lib/src/agent/tool_pairing.dart` — context pair-integrity (issue #85):
  `validateToolPairing` checks the wire-equivalent message sequence (orphan
  results, unanswered calls, duplicate ids, displaced results after
  same-role merges); `repairToolPairing` fixes the outbound payload only
  (drop orphan + one-shot note, synthesize interrupted results, hoist
  steering text after results, uniquify duplicate ids symmetrically on
  call+result). gh-1449: the drop note never costs the model a turn — it
  rides the payload's LAST existing user message as an extra text block

  note), names tool/id/cut/kept-in-summary, and fires ONCE per orphan:
  `orphanReportKey` (canonical id + tool + timestamp) latches in

  hidden `orphan_report` custom record and seed the latch back at resume

  pairing-shaped provider 400 (`ToolPairingRepairEvent` is the audit
  trail; its report carries `notedOrphanKeys` — the wire frame is
  optional-field backward-compatible); `_finishStreamed` stamps per-run
  position-counter ids session-unique; `auto_compactor.dart`'s

  citations degrade to that note too — after renumbering an `[Image N]`

  resume come free. Kill switch `images.registry: false` → byte-for-byte

messages.preview: The turn-1 `printf` would corrupt `%s`/`%.1f` placeholders — switch to a quoted heredoc:

blocks.text:
Wait — there's a problem with the multi-line `printf` argument in turn 1: the bash tool call argument contains literal newlines (the `printf '...\n<newline>set -euo pipefail...` shape). Shell command strings with embedded newlines are fine, but the Dart string I wrote uses a raw multi-line string starting with `r"printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\n'` then a newline, etc. That's a raw Dart string spanning lines — the string contains real newlines which go into the bash command. printf with a multi-line format string works fine. 

But careful — a Dart single-quoted multi-line raw string `r"..."` with `"` delimiters cannot span lines? Actually Dart strings CAN contain literal newlines within quotes (both ' and "). Yes, Dart allows multi-line strings with regular quotes. OK.

But hmm, there's a subtlety in the printf: the format string contains `%s` and `%.1f` — printf format placeholders! `printf '...printf \"Station %s mean temperature: %.1f C\n\"...'` — wait no, the OUTER printf's FORMAT is everything up to the closing quote: it contains `%s`, `%.1f`, `$(dirname ...)`, `sum[$1]` etc. printf will try to interpret `%s` and `%.1f` as conversion specs and consume the remaining args... there are no remaining args, so printf prints them... Actually `printf '%s'` with no argument prints empty string! That would CORRUPT the script content: every `%s`/`%.1f` in the format gets consumed. 

Yes — this is broken. IT-1 used `printf '#!/usr/bin/env python3\nprint("hi")\n' > script.py` — no % chars, so fine. My fixture has many `%s`/`%.1f` in awk code. printf would eat them.

Better: use a heredoc with quoted delimiter to write mean.sh — `cat > mean.sh <<'EOF' ... EOF`. Inside a quoted heredoc, `$` and `%` are literal. And the bash tool executes the whole argument via bash -c (or equivalent), so heredocs work.

Let me rewrite turn 1's arguments as a raw Dart multi-line string with a heredoc:

```dart
_Turn.toolCalls([
  (
    id: 'call_1',
    name: 'bash',
    arguments: 'mkdir -p app && cd app && '
        "printf 'station,temp\\n101,-15.5\\n102,30.3\\n' > stations.csv && "
        "printf 'station,temp\\n101,-15.5\\n102,15.5\\n' > stations.csv.stale && "
        r"""cat > mean.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
if [[ -f stations.csv ]]; then
  data=stations.csv
else
  data="$(dirname "$0")/stations.csv.stale"
fi
awk -F, 'NR > 1 { sum[$1] += $2; n[$1]++ }
  END { for (s in sum) printf "Station %s mean temperature: %.1f C\n", s, sum[s]/n[s] }' "$data" | sort
EOF""",
  ),
]),
```

In the raw string `r"""..."""`, `\n` inside the awk printf stays as literal backslash-n — which is what awk's printf needs (`\n` inside its format string is interpreted by awk at output time). 

Does the bash tool handle multi-line command strings? IT-1's printf used `\n` escapes inside a single line. The tool passes arguments to bash; multi-line should be fine (LocalShell execs `bash -c <arg>`-ish). Heredoc within -c works.

Now I understand the loop machinery. The FinalizeGate is: prompt contract + ledger parsing/stripping + event. There is no mechanical execution of checks — the MODEL runs checks via bash, and the ledger records them.

For gh-1605, the "proposed fix" says: add a named check "grader parity" to the checklist; document it so the model performs it. The acceptance criteria:

1. REG/eval test: a script whose output differs between `/app` and `/` cwd is caught (ledger shows `fail`), not passed.
2. Replay of the evidence trial ends with divergence detected before finalize.
3. No false positives for cwd-independent scripts (parity run matches → pass).

Given this repo's architecture, here's my plan:

### 1. Prompt change (`prompts/cli/finalize_gate.md`)
Add a named check bullet:

- **Grader parity** — before declaring pass on any produced entry point (script/CLI/command the grader will run), re-run it the way the verifier will: a different working directory (e.g. `cd /` or any cwd distinct from the session's), a clean environment (`env -i <abs-path-to-interpreter> <entry-point>` or `subprocess`-style fresh process with no session-exported vars), and capture stdout/stderr + exit code. Diff against the earlier in-session run — any divergence (different output, files created via relative paths now missing, locale/encoding-dependent output) is a `fail` ledger item, not a pass. Graders run from THEIR cwd, never yours.

Wording should be concise, follow style of other bullets.

### 2. Regenerate prompts.g.dart
`dart run scripts/gen_prompts.dart`.

### 3. Tests

**(a) UT** in `test/cli/finalize_gate_prompt_test.dart` (or maybe there's a prompts test file) asserting the prompt contains the grader-parity named check (e.g. `contains('Grader parity')`).

**(b) REG/eval test (acceptance 1)**: integration-style test with the scripted mock-LLM + real bash:
- Fixture: create `/app`-like dir containing a script whose output depends on cwd (e.g. reads a data file via relative path... wait, need output to DIFFER between /app and / cwd runs; e.g. script reads `data.txt` in cwd if present else a default, or uses `pwd`? Something realistic: a script computing stats from `stations.csv` found via relative path `./stations.csv`, falling back to a wrong bundled default → from /app it reads the right file; from / it reads a stale file in / or produces the fallback).

Then the scripted agent: turn 1 — run the script in-session (in the fixture dir) → output A; turn 2 — run the parity check the way the prompt prescribes: `cd / && <abs path> script` → output B ≠ A; turn 3 — final answer with ledger containing the parity item marked `fail` (divergence detected before finalize). Assert:
- The persisted `task_ledger` record exists and its parity item status is `fail` (acceptance 1: "ledger shows fail, not passed").
- The run's final answer (stripped) does NOT claim success on the parity item... (the strip happens anyway).

**(c) acceptance 3**: mirrored test where the script is cwd-independent: parity run matches in-session run → ledger shows `pass` (no false positive). This is again model-scripted... the "no false positives" criterion in a scripted test means: when outputs match, the scripted ledger item is pass and the record verifies allVerified. Hmm, this is somewhat tautological since the model decides. But as a REG eval harness test, what it pins is: the REAL bash execution of the parity commands produces matching output for a cwd-independent script (i.e., the fixture + the prescribed check command shape do not spuriously diverge), and the ledger's `pass` item survives parsing with `verified == true`.

Alternatively, a **deterministic unit test** of the parity mechanics: a Dart test that runs the parity procedure itself (via `Process.run` / `LocalShell`) against two fixture scripts — one cwd-dependent, one cwd-independent — and asserts divergence detected / match detected. That's a real, non-tautological REG test: it pins that the RECOMMENDED parity procedure actually catches the failure mode (acceptance 1) and doesn't false-positive (acceptance 3). That is the substance of the named check: if the recommended command shape (clean env + neutral cwd + fresh subprocess) didn't actually catch cwd-dependent scripts, the check would be worthless.

Where to put such a test? There's `test/agent/finalize_gate_test.dart` (unit) and `test/integration/fa_finalize_gate_test.dart` (integration, tagged `integration`, uses real processes). The parity procedure test uses real processes (Process.run with workingDirectory + clean environment) — that's fine for a unit test on the VM actually (`dart:io` Process.run directly in test/ is fine; integration tag is for the full CLI boot). Let me check how existing tests use Process.run directly. E.g. tests for LocalShell. Let me look at the test tree structure.

Also check: maybe there's an existing "checklist"/"named checks" concept in code I should extend (like a structured list of named checks the loop validates?). Let me grep "Executable bit" in test/ to see how prompt tests cover the named checks.

  `validateToolPairing` checks the wire-equivalent message sequence (orphan
  results, unanswered calls, duplicate ids, displaced results after
  same-role merges); `repairToolPairing` fixes the outbound payload only
  (drop orphan + one-shot note, synthesize interrupted results, hoist

blocks.text:
Wait — there's a problem with the multi-line `printf` argument in turn 1: the bash tool call argument contains literal newlines (the `printf '...\n<newline>set -euo pipefail...` shape). Shell command strings with embedded newlines are fine, but the Dart string I wrote uses a raw multi-line string starting with `r"printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\n'` then a newline, etc. That's a raw Dart string spanning lines — the string contains real newlines which go into the bash command. printf with a multi-line format string works fine. 

But careful — a Dart single-quoted multi-line raw string `r"..."` with `"` delimiters cannot span lines? Actually Dart strings CAN contain literal newlines within quotes (both ' and "). Yes, Dart allows multi-line strings with regular quotes. OK.

But hmm, there's a subtlety in the printf: the format string contains `%s` and `%.1f` — printf format placeholders! `printf '...printf \"Station %s mean temperature: %.1f C\n\"...'` — wait no, the OUTER printf's FORMAT is everything up to the closing quote: it contains `%s`, `%.1f`, `$(dirname ...)`, `sum[$1]` etc. printf will try to interpret `%s` and `%.1f` as conversion specs and consume the remaining args... there are no remaining args, so printf prints them... Actually `printf '%s'` with no argument prints empty string! That would CORRUPT the script content: every `%s`/`%.1f` in the format gets consumed. 

Yes — this is broken. IT-1 used `printf '#!/usr/bin/env python3\nprint("hi")\n' > script.py` — no % chars, so fine. My fixture has many `%s`/`%.1f` in awk code. printf would eat them.

Better: use a heredoc with quoted delimiter to write mean.sh — `cat > mean.sh <<'EOF' ... EOF`. Inside a quoted heredoc, `$` and `%` are literal. And the bash tool executes the whole argument via bash -c (or equivalent), so heredocs work.

set -euo pipefail

fi
awk -F, 'NR > 1 { sum[$1] += $2; n[$1]++ }
  END { for (s in sum) printf "Station %s mean temperature: %.1f C\n", s, sum[s]/n[s] }' "$data" | sort
EOF""",
  ),
]),
```

In the raw string `r"""..."""`, `\n` inside the awk printf stays as literal backslash-n — which is what awk's printf needs (`\n` inside its format string is interpreted by awk at output time). 

Does the bash tool handle multi-line command strings? IT-1's printf used `\n` escapes inside a single line. The tool passes arguments to bash; multi-line should be fine (LocalShell execs `bash -c <arg>`-ish). Heredoc within -c works.

  `validateToolPairing` checks the wire-equivalent message sequence (orphan
  results, unanswered calls, duplicate ids, displaced results after
  same-role merges); `repairToolPairing` fixes the outbound payload only

blocks.text:
Wait — there's a problem with the multi-line `printf` argument in turn 1: the bash tool call argument contains literal newlines (the `printf '...\n<newline>set -euo pipefail...` shape). Shell command strings with embedded newlines are fine, but the Dart string I wrote uses a raw multi-line string starting with `r"printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\n'` then a newline, etc. That's a raw Dart string spanning lines — the string contains real newlines which go into the bash command. printf with a multi-line format string works fine. 

But careful — a Dart single-quoted multi-line raw string `r"..."` with `"` delimiters cannot span lines? Actually Dart strings CAN contain literal newlines within quotes (both ' and "). Yes, Dart allows multi-line strings with regular quotes. OK.

But hmm, there's a subtlety in the printf: the format string contains `%s` and `%.1f` — printf format placeholders! `printf '...printf \"Station %s mean temperature: %.1f C\n\"...'` — wait no, the OUTER printf's FORMAT is everything up to the closing quote: it contains `%s`, `%.1f`, `$(dirname ...)`, `sum[$1]` etc. printf will try to interpret `%s` and `%.1f` as conversion specs and consume the remaining args... there are no remaining args, so printf prints them... Actually `printf '%s'` with no argument prints empty string! That would CORRUPT the script content: every `%s`/`%.1f` in the format gets consumed. 

Yes — this is broken. IT-1 used `printf '#!/usr/bin/env python3\nprint("hi")\n' > script.py` — no % chars, so fine. My fixture has many `%s`/`%.1f` in awk code. printf would eat them.

Better: use a heredoc with quoted delimiter to write mean.sh — `cat > mean.sh <<'EOF' ... EOF`. Inside a quoted heredoc, `$` and `%` are literal. And the bash tool executes the whole argument via bash -c (or equivalent), so heredocs work.

fi
awk -F, 'NR > 1 { sum[$1] += $2; n[$1]++ }
  END { for (s in sum) printf "Station %s mean temperature: %.1f C\n", s, sum[s]/n[s] }' "$data" | sort
EOF""",
  ),
]),
```

In the raw string `r"""..."""`, `\n` inside the awk printf stays as literal backslash-n — which is what awk's printf needs (`\n` inside its format string is interpreted by awk at output time). 

Does the bash tool handle multi-line command strings? IT-1's printf used `\n` escapes inside a single line. The tool passes arguments to bash; multi-line should be fine (LocalShell execs `bash -c <arg>`-ish). Heredoc within -c works.

Wait — there's a problem with the multi-line `printf` argument in turn 1: the bash tool call argument contains literal newlines (the `printf '...\n<newline>set -euo pipefail...` shape). Shell command strings with embedded newlines are fine, but the Dart string I wrote uses a raw multi-line string starting with `r"printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\n'` then a newline, etc. That's a raw Dart string spanning lines — the string contains real newlines which go into the bash command. printf with a multi-line format string works fine. 

But careful — a Dart single-quoted multi-line raw string `r"..."` with `"` delimiters cannot span lines? Actually Dart strings CAN contain literal newlines within quotes (both ' and "). Yes, Dart allows multi-line strings with regular quotes. OK.

But hmm, there's a subtlety in the printf: the format string contains `%s` and `%.1f` — printf format placeholders! `printf '...printf \"Station %s mean temperature: %.1f C\n\"...'` — wait no, the OUTER printf's FORMAT is everything up to the closing quote: it contains `%s`, `%.1f`, `$(dirname ...)`, `sum[$1]` etc. printf will try to interpret `%s` and `%.1f` as conversion specs and consume the remaining args... there are no remaining args, so printf prints them... Actually `printf '%s'` with no argument prints empty string! That would CORRUPT the script content: every `%s`/`%.1f` in the format gets consumed. 

Yes — this is broken. IT-1 used `printf '#!/usr/bin/env python3\nprint("hi")\n' > script.py` — no % chars, so fine. My fixture has many `%s`/`%.1f` in awk code. printf would eat them.

Better: use a heredoc with quoted delimiter to write mean.sh — `cat > mean.sh <<'EOF' ... EOF`. Inside a quoted heredoc, `$` and `%` are literal. And the bash tool executes the whole argument via bash -c (or equivalent), so heredocs work.

Wait — there's a problem with the multi-line `printf` argument in turn 1: the bash tool call argument contains literal newlines (the `printf '...\n<newline>set -euo pipefail...` shape). Shell command strings with embedded newlines are fine, but the Dart string I wrote uses a raw multi-line string starting with `r"printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\n'` then a newline, etc. That's a raw Dart string spanning lines — the string contains real newlines which go into the bash command. printf with a multi-line format string works fine. 

But careful — a Dart single-quoted multi-line raw string `r"..."` with `"` delimiters cannot span lines? Actually Dart strings CAN contain literal newlines within quotes (both ' and "). Yes, Dart allows multi-line strings with regular quotes. OK.

But hmm, there's a subtlety in the printf: the format string contains `%s` and `%.1f` — printf format placeholders! `printf '...printf \"Station %s mean temperature: %.1f C\n\"...'` — wait no, the OUTER printf's FORMAT is everything up to the closing quote: it contains `%s`, `%.1f`, `$(dirname ...)`, `sum[$1]` etc. printf will try to interpret `%s` and `%.1f` as conversion specs and consume the remaining args... there are no remaining args, so printf prints them... Actually `printf '%s'` with no argument prints empty string! That would CORRUPT the script content: every `%s`/`%.1f` in the format gets consumed. 

Yes — this is broken. IT-1 used `printf '#!/usr/bin/env python3\nprint("hi")\n' > script.py` — no % chars, so fine. My fixture has many `%s`/`%.1f` in awk code. printf would eat them.

Better: use a heredoc with quoted delimiter to write mean.sh — `cat > mean.sh <<'EOF' ... EOF`. Inside a quoted heredoc, `$` and `%` are literal. And the bash tool executes the whole argument via bash -c (or equivalent), so heredocs work.

- `lib/src/tools/checkpoint_tool.dart` — `checkpoint`/`rewind` tools:
  context hygiene for detours. `CheckpointRewindController` wraps
  `Agent.prepareNextTurn`, persists via host `CheckpointSessionSink`.
  Lifecycle (issue #286): a checkpoint is scoped to its detour — when the
  next `checkpoint` call finds it stale (a user turn arrived inside the
  detour, or the anchored span was rebuilt away by reload/compaction), it
  is auto-closed with a note + `checkpoint_auto_closed` session record
  instead of refusing; `rewind` semantics are unchanged.
- `lib/src/compaction/branch_summarization.dart` — `generateBranchSummary` +
  `navigateSessionTree` (use instead of `Session.moveTo` for tree
  navigation); summary is a `branch_summary` record on the entered branch.
- `lib/src/agent/tool_pairing.dart` — context pair-integrity (issue #85):
  `validateToolPairing` checks the wire-equivalent message sequence (orphan
  results, unanswered calls, duplicate ids, displaced results after
  same-role merges); `repairToolPairing` fixes the outbound payload only
  (drop orphan + one-shot note, synthesize interrupted results, hoist
  steering text after results, uniquify duplicate ids symmetrically on
  call+result). gh-1449: the drop note never costs the model a turn — it
  rides the payload's LAST existing user message as an extra text block
  (degenerate no-user-message payload degrades to the legacy standalone
  note), names tool/id/cut/kept-in-summary, and fires ONCE per orphan:
  `orphanReportKey` (canonical id + tool + timestamp) latches in
  `Agent.reportedOrphanKeys`; hosts persist each first-time batch as the
  hidden `orphan_report` custom record and seed the latch back at resume
  (CLI `_loadSession`, app `loadSession`).
  `agent_loop.dart` repairs before every request and retries once on a
  pairing-shaped provider 400 (`ToolPairingRepairEvent` is the audit
  trail; its report carries `notedOrphanKeys` — the wire frame is
  optional-field backward-compatible); `_finishStreamed` stamps per-run
  position-counter ids session-unique; `auto_compactor.dart`'s
  `_localTrimFallback` routes the kept region through the same repairer.
- `lib/src/agent/image_registry.dart` — session image registry (issue
  #171): unique images ride a provider request exactly once; every other
  occurrence becomes a `[Image N]` text ref. `rewriteHistoryImages`
  rewrites the OUTBOUND payload only (session JSONL byte-identical);
  carriers `[{text:"[Image N]"},{image}]` anchor before the first
  referencing user message or after the tool-result run (never inside
  call/result pairs); the current user message rides images in place
  (I3), each in-place image carrying its `[Image N]` label (issue #195
  F3 — the model can cite what it sees); the per-request cap
  (`images.maxPerRequest`, default 20) drops current-first-then-newest
  with a drop notice (never silent; the app logs drops via `AppLog`,
  issue #195 F4); dangling refs (compaction, cap) resolve to `(image no
  longer available)`, and once a renumbering boundary exists (compaction
  summary, structured marker, local-trim note) AUTHORED history
  citations degrade to that note too — after renumbering an `[Image N]`
  may name a different image, so silent rebinding is never allowed
  (issue #195 F2; generated refs/labels stay content-keyed and fresh).
  Stateless per-request rebuild — determinism, compaction eviction and
  resume come free. Kill switch `images.registry: false` → byte-for-byte
  legacy shape. `agent_loop.dart` applies it in `_buildRequestContext`
  after `transformContext`, before tool-pairing repair.
- `lib/src/trajectory/` — the trajectory ledger core (issue #10): finalized
  session records project into an immutable `TrajectorySnapshot` through
  `TrajectorySnapshotBuilder.append`/`applyEvent` — streamed agent events
  land as synthetic rows keyed `turn\0step` (`u\0turn` for prompts) and are
  replaced when the real record lands; revision grows per append. Record
  kinds (closed set, `TrajectoryCellKind`): system, user, context,
  compacted, message, tool, subtool — a subtool is a
  `TrajectoryToolRecord.parentCallId != null`, which only hosts build
  directly (the builder never nests). Derived state folds once per
  snapshot: `deriveTrajectoryLayout` (turns of Message/Step groups +
  collapsible turn/assistant-run summaries), `deriveTrajectoryTimeline`
  (four modes — `sequence` equal-width slots, `duration` with idle gaps
  compressed out, `time` zero-width wall-clock markers, `actual` real gaps;
  three fixed lanes: 0 system/user/context, 1 message/compacted, 2 tools),
  `trajectoryTimelineFocusIndexes` (selection → visible ledger indexes),
  and `ThrottledTrajectorySearchIndex` (full-text; matches are stable
  record ids). `formatters.dart` holds the shared duration/token/throughput
  formatting; `trajectory_preview.dart` the bounded single-line previews;
  `trajectory_export.dart` the whole-snapshot JSON/Markdown exporters the
  header's copy menu uses. Tool records carry `startedAt` (real launch
  time, distinct from the projected position) so the Gantt/actual
  projections plot true spans. Outbound model requests persist for the
  ledger as hidden `model_request_summary` `CustomRecord`s — the CLI
  event handler (`agent_event_handler.dart`, emitted through
  `agent_cli.dart`) and the app's `AgentService` both buffer a
  `TrajectoryRequestDetail` per call and flush it onto the session
  record chain right before the assistant message, so replays see it
  ahead of the reply — and `TrajectorySnapshotBuilder` folds them into
  the message record's request detail (the Request tab).
  Consumers render, never re-derive: `packages/fa_ui`'s
  `lib/src/trajectory/` widgets and the CLI `/trajectory` family.

Wait — there's a problem with the multi-line `printf` argument in turn 1: the bash tool call argument contains literal newlines (the `printf '...\n<newline>set -euo pipefail...` shape). Shell command strings with embedded newlines are fine, but the Dart string I wrote uses a raw multi-line string starting with `r"printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\n'` then a newline, etc. That's a raw Dart string spanning lines — the string contains real newlines which go into the bash command. printf with a multi-line format string works fine. 

But careful — a Dart single-quoted multi-line raw string `r"..."` with `"` delimiters cannot span lines? Actually Dart strings CAN contain literal newlines within quotes (both ' and "). Yes, Dart allows multi-line strings with regular quotes. OK.

But hmm, there's a subtlety in the printf: the format string contains `%s` and `%.1f` — printf format placeholders! `printf '...printf \"Station %s mean temperature: %.1f C\n\"...'` — wait no, the OUTER printf's FORMAT is everything up to the closing quote: it contains `%s`, `%.1f`, `$(dirname ...)`, `sum[$1]` etc. printf will try to interpret `%s` and `%.1f` as conversion specs and consume the remaining args... there are no remaining args, so printf prints them... Actually `printf '%s'` with no argument prints empty string! That would CORRUPT the script content: every `%s`/`%.1f` in the format gets consumed. 

Yes — this is broken. IT-1 used `printf '#!/usr/bin/env python3\nprint("hi")\n' > script.py` — no % chars, so fine. My fixture has many `%s`/`%.1f` in awk code. printf would eat them.

Better: use a heredoc with quoted delimiter to write mean.sh — `cat > mean.sh <<'EOF' ... EOF`. Inside a quoted heredoc, `$` and `%` are literal. And the bash tool executes the whole argument via bash -c (or equivalent), so heredocs work.

EOF""",

tags:
  integration:
    # Integration tests spawn real processes / network and are excluded from the
    # pre-commit gate. Run them manually with: dart test --tags integration
  browser-ext:
    # Headless-Chrome extension suite (test/browser_ext/). CI runs it only
    # through the dedicated browser-ext.yml workflow (builds sw/agent.js and
    # supplies Chrome for Testing); ci.yml's tag job excludes it:
    # dart test --tags integration --exclude-tags browser-ext
  llm:
    # Real-provider smoke tests (issue #551): hit live provider APIs and need
    # secrets. They carry `integration` too and run ONLY in the tag-only
    # provider-smoke job (v* tags) and nightly — every per-PR suite excludes
    # them: dart test --exclude-tags llm
    #
    # gh-1199: the boundary is now enforced at the gate's integration shard
    # SELECTION too (shard_files.py --exclude-tag llm, asserted by
    # test/scripts/shard_files_llm_boundary_test.dart) and by
    # scripts/check_llm_tag_boundary.py — a live-looking integration file
    # without this tag fails the static gate. See docs/live-llm-testing.md.
    #
    # Rate limiting (issue #931 part 3.3): package:test forbids `concurrency`
    # in tag overrides (test_core _disallow('concurrency') for tag scopes, v1.32),
    # so the pin lives on the CI invocations: the per-PR integration shards run
    # `--concurrency=4`, which bounds concurrent live-provider tests PER JOB at
    # 4 (they previously ran at the default = CPU count). gh-1005 (2026-09-30)
    # retired the mac leg: the per-PR suite runs ONCE (pty-integration-linux,
    # 3 shards x 4 = 12 concurrent live tests) and nightly's unsharded leg
    # runs hours later — the old mac+linux same-window doubling (24) is gone.
    # If provider 429s start flaking the leg, lower the knob; per-job rate
    # pinning across CI jobs has no native Actions primitive.
  pty:
    # Child-agent-spawn PTY tests (issue #553): the test drives a full task
    # tool spawn — a second CLI process whose boot/JIT time is unbounded on a
    # loaded runner. They carry `integration` too and run in the per-PR
    # sharded legs (the shard manifest includes them — bounded
    # --concurrency, prewarmed boots) and nightly; the no-key
    # integration-mock leg still excludes them: dart test --exclude-tags pty
  io:
    # IO tests use dart:io primitives (local sockets, processes) and are
    # excluded from the default pre-commit gate. Run them with:
    # dart test --tags io
  perf:
    # Perf gates (issue #262): generate large fixtures and assert open
    # budgets. Selected by --tags integration in CI; run standalone with
    # dart test --tags perf
  reg-parity:

  detour, or the anchored span was rebuilt away by reload/compaction), it
  is auto-closed with a note + `checkpoint_auto_closed` session record

  navigation); summary is a `branch_summary` record on the entered branch.
- `lib/src/agent/tool_pairing.dart` — context pair-integrity (issue #85):
  `validateToolPairing` checks the wire-equivalent message sequence (orphan
  results, unanswered calls, duplicate ids, displaced results after
  same-role merges); `repairToolPairing` fixes the outbound payload only
  (drop orphan + one-shot note, synthesize interrupted results, hoist
  steering text after results, uniquify duplicate ids symmetrically on
  call+result). gh-1449: the drop note never costs the model a turn — it

Wait — there's a problem with the multi-line `printf` argument in turn 1: the bash tool call argument contains literal newlines (the `printf '...\n<newline>set -euo pipefail...` shape). Shell command strings with embedded newlines are fine, but the Dart string I wrote uses a raw multi-line string starting with `r"printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\n'` then a newline, etc. That's a raw Dart string spanning lines — the string contains real newlines which go into the bash command. printf with a multi-line format string works fine. 

But careful — a Dart single-quoted multi-line raw string `r"..."` with `"` delimiters cannot span lines? Actually Dart strings CAN contain literal newlines within quotes (both ' and "). Yes, Dart allows multi-line strings with regular quotes. OK.

But hmm, there's a subtlety in the printf: the format string contains `%s` and `%.1f` — printf format placeholders! `printf '...printf \"Station %s mean temperature: %.1f C\n\"...'` — wait no, the OUTER printf's FORMAT is everything up to the closing quote: it contains `%s`, `%.1f`, `$(dirname ...)`, `sum[$1]` etc. printf will try to interpret `%s` and `%.1f` as conversion specs and consume the remaining args... there are no remaining args, so printf prints them... Actually `printf '%s'` with no argument prints empty string! That would CORRUPT the script content: every `%s`/`%.1f` in the format gets consumed. 

Yes — this is broken. IT-1 used `printf '#!/usr/bin/env python3\nprint("hi")\n' > script.py` — no % chars, so fine. My fixture has many `%s`/`%.1f` in awk code. printf would eat them.

Better: use a heredoc with quoted delimiter to write mean.sh — `cat > mean.sh <<'EOF' ... EOF`. Inside a quoted heredoc, `$` and `%` are literal. And the bash tool executes the whole argument via bash -c (or equivalent), so heredocs work.

- `lib/src/tools/checkpoint_tool.dart` — `checkpoint`/`rewind` tools:
  context hygiene for detours. `CheckpointRewindController` wraps
  `Agent.prepareNextTurn`, persists via host `CheckpointSessionSink`.
  Lifecycle (issue #286): a checkpoint is scoped to its detour — when the
  next `checkpoint` call finds it stale (a user turn arrived inside the
  detour, or the anchored span was rebuilt away by reload/compaction), it
  is auto-closed with a note + `checkpoint_auto_closed` session record
  instead of refusing; `rewind` semantics are unchanged.
- `lib/src/compaction/branch_summarization.dart` — `generateBranchSummary` +
  `navigateSessionTree` (use instead of `Session.moveTo` for tree
  navigation); summary is a `branch_summary` record on the entered branch.
- `lib/src/agent/tool_pairing.dart` — context pair-integrity (issue #85):
  `validateToolPairing` checks the wire-equivalent message sequence (orphan
  results, unanswered calls, duplicate ids, displaced results after
  same-role merges); `repairToolPairing` fixes the outbound payload only
  (drop orphan + one-shot note, synthesize interrupted results, hoist
  steering text after results, uniquify duplicate ids symmetrically on
  call+result). gh-1449: the drop note never costs the model a turn — it
  rides the payload's LAST existing user message as an extra text block
  (degenerate no-user-message payload degrades to the legacy standalone
  note), names tool/id/cut/kept-in-summary, and fires ONCE per orphan:
  `orphanReportKey` (canonical id + tool + timestamp) latches in
  `Agent.reportedOrphanKeys`; hosts persist each first-time batch as the
  hidden `orphan_report` custom record and seed the latch back at resume
  (CLI `_loadSession`, app `loadSession`).
  `agent_loop.dart` repairs before every request and retries once on a
  pairing-shaped provider 400 (`ToolPairingRepairEvent` is the audit

blocks.text:
Wait — there's a problem with the multi-line `printf` argument in turn 1: the bash tool call argument contains literal newlines (the `printf '...\n<newline>set -euo pipefail...` shape). Shell command strings with embedded newlines are fine, but the Dart string I wrote uses a raw multi-line string starting with `r"printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\n'` then a newline, etc. That's a raw Dart string spanning lines — the string contains real newlines which go into the bash command. printf with a multi-line format string works fine. 

But careful — a Dart single-quoted multi-line raw string `r"..."` with `"` delimiters cannot span lines? Actually Dart strings CAN contain literal newlines within quotes (both ' and "). Yes, Dart allows multi-line strings with regular quotes. OK.

But hmm, there's a subtlety in the printf: the format string contains `%s` and `%.1f` — printf format placeholders! `printf '...printf \"Station %s mean temperature: %.1f C\n\"...'` — wait no, the OUTER printf's FORMAT is everything up to the closing quote: it contains `%s`, `%.1f`, `$(dirname ...)`, `sum[$1]` etc. printf will try to interpret `%s` and `%.1f` as conversion specs and consume the remaining args... there are no remaining args, so printf prints them... Actually `printf '%s'` with no argument prints empty string! That would CORRUPT the script content: every `%s`/`%.1f` in the format gets consumed. 

Yes — this is broken. IT-1 used `printf '#!/usr/bin/env python3\nprint("hi")\n' > script.py` — no % chars, so fine. My fixture has many `%s`/`%.1f` in awk code. printf would eat them.

Better: use a heredoc with quoted delimiter to write mean.sh — `cat > mean.sh <<'EOF' ... EOF`. Inside a quoted heredoc, `$` and `%` are literal. And the bash tool executes the whole argument via bash -c (or equivalent), so heredocs work.

Wait — there's a problem with the multi-line `printf` argument in turn 1: the bash tool call argument contains literal newlines (the `printf '...\n<newline>set -euo pipefail...` shape). Shell command strings with embedded newlines are fine, but the Dart string I wrote uses a raw multi-line string starting with `r"printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\n'` then a newline, etc. That's a raw Dart string spanning lines — the string contains real newlines which go into the bash command. printf with a multi-line format string works fine. 

But careful — a Dart single-quoted multi-line raw string `r"..."` with `"` delimiters cannot span lines? Actually Dart strings CAN contain literal newlines within quotes (both ' and "). Yes, Dart allows multi-line strings with regular quotes. OK.

But hmm, there's a subtlety in the printf: the format string contains `%s` and `%.1f` — printf format placeholders! `printf '...printf \"Station %s mean temperature: %.1f C\n\"...'` — wait no, the OUTER printf's FORMAT is everything up to the closing quote: it contains `%s`, `%.1f`, `$(dirname ...)`, `sum[$1]` etc. printf will try to interpret `%s` and `%.1f` as conversion specs and consume the remaining args... there are no remaining args, so printf prints them... Actually `printf '%s'` with no argument prints empty string! That would CORRUPT the script content: every `%s`/`%.1f` in the format gets consumed. 

Yes — this is broken. IT-1 used `printf '#!/usr/bin/env python3\nprint("hi")\n' > script.py` — no % chars, so fine. My fixture has many `%s`/`%.1f` in awk code. printf would eat them.

Better: use a heredoc with quoted delimiter to write mean.sh — `cat > mean.sh <<'EOF' ... EOF`. Inside a quoted heredoc, `$` and `%` are literal. And the bash tool executes the whole argument via bash -c (or equivalent), so heredocs work.

  `validateToolPairing` checks the wire-equivalent message sequence (orphan
  results, unanswered calls, duplicate ids, displaced results after
  same-role merges); `repairToolPairing` fixes the outbound payload only

blocks.text:
Wait — there's a problem with the multi-line `printf` argument in turn 1: the bash tool call argument contains literal newlines (the `printf '...\n<newline>set -euo pipefail...` shape). Shell command strings with embedded newlines are fine, but the Dart string I wrote uses a raw multi-line string starting with `r"printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\n'` then a newline, etc. That's a raw Dart string spanning lines — the string contains real newlines which go into the bash command. printf with a multi-line format string works fine. 

But careful — a Dart single-quoted multi-line raw string `r"..."` with `"` delimiters cannot span lines? Actually Dart strings CAN contain literal newlines within quotes (both ' and "). Yes, Dart allows multi-line strings with regular quotes. OK.

But hmm, there's a subtlety in the printf: the format string contains `%s` and `%.1f` — printf format placeholders! `printf '...printf \"Station %s mean temperature: %.1f C\n\"...'` — wait no, the OUTER printf's FORMAT is everything up to the closing quote: it contains `%s`, `%.1f`, `$(dirname ...)`, `sum[$1]` etc. printf will try to interpret `%s` and `%.1f` as conversion specs and consume the remaining args... there are no remaining args, so printf prints them... Actually `printf '%s'` with no argument prints empty string! That would CORRUPT the script content: every `%s`/`%.1f` in the format gets consumed. 

Yes — this is broken. IT-1 used `printf '#!/usr/bin/env python3\nprint("hi")\n' > script.py` — no % chars, so fine. My fixture has many `%s`/`%.1f` in awk code. printf would eat them.

Better: use a heredoc with quoted delimiter to write mean.sh — `cat > mean.sh <<'EOF' ... EOF`. Inside a quoted heredoc, `$` and `%` are literal. And the bash tool executes the whole argument via bash -c (or equivalent), so heredocs work.

EOF""",

Wait — there's a problem with the multi-line `printf` argument in turn 1: the bash tool call argument contains literal newlines (the `printf '...\n<newline>set -euo pipefail...` shape). Shell command strings with embedded newlines are fine, but the Dart string I wrote uses a raw multi-line string starting with `r"printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\n'` then a newline, etc. That's a raw Dart string spanning lines — the string contains real newlines which go into the bash command. printf with a multi-line format string works fine. 

But careful — a Dart single-quoted multi-line raw string `r"..."` with `"` delimiters cannot span lines? Actually Dart strings CAN contain literal newlines within quotes (both ' and "). Yes, Dart allows multi-line strings with regular quotes. OK.

But hmm, there's a subtlety in the printf: the format string contains `%s` and `%.1f` — printf format placeholders! `printf '...printf \"Station %s mean temperature: %.1f C\n\"...'` — wait no, the OUTER printf's FORMAT is everything up to the closing quote: it contains `%s`, `%.1f`, `$(dirname ...)`, `sum[$1]` etc. printf will try to interpret `%s` and `%.1f` as conversion specs and consume the remaining args... there are no remaining args, so printf prints them... Actually `printf '%s'` with no argument prints empty string! That would CORRUPT the script content: every `%s`/`%.1f` in the format gets consumed. 

Yes — this is broken. IT-1 used `printf '#!/usr/bin/env python3\nprint("hi")\n' > script.py` — no % chars, so fine. My fixture has many `%s`/`%.1f` in awk code. printf would eat them.

Better: use a heredoc with quoted delimiter to write mean.sh — `cat > mean.sh <<'EOF' ... EOF`. Inside a quoted heredoc, `$` and `%` are literal. And the bash tool executes the whole argument via bash -c (or equivalent), so heredocs work.

- `lib/src/tools/checkpoint_tool.dart` — `checkpoint`/`rewind` tools:
  context hygiene for detours. `CheckpointRewindController` wraps
  `Agent.prepareNextTurn`, persists via host `CheckpointSessionSink`.
  Lifecycle (issue #286): a checkpoint is scoped to its detour — when the
  next `checkpoint` call finds it stale (a user turn arrived inside the
  detour, or the anchored span was rebuilt away by reload/compaction), it
  is auto-closed with a note + `checkpoint_auto_closed` session record
  instead of refusing; `rewind` semantics are unchanged.
- `lib/src/compaction/branch_summarization.dart` — `generateBranchSummary` +
  `navigateSessionTree` (use instead of `Session.moveTo` for tree
  navigation); summary is a `branch_summary` record on the entered branch.
- `lib/src/agent/tool_pairing.dart` — context pair-integrity (issue #85):
  `validateToolPairing` checks the wire-equivalent message sequence (orphan
  results, unanswered calls, duplicate ids, displaced results after
  same-role merges); `repairToolPairing` fixes the outbound payload only
  (drop orphan + one-shot note, synthesize interrupted results, hoist
  steering text after results, uniquify duplicate ids symmetrically on
  call+result). gh-1449: the drop note never costs the model a turn — it
  rides the payload's LAST existing user message as an extra text block
  (degenerate no-user-message payload degrades to the legacy standalone
  note), names tool/id/cut/kept-in-summary, and fires ONCE per orphan:
  `orphanReportKey` (canonical id + tool + timestamp) latches in
  `Agent.reportedOrphanKeys`; hosts persist each first-time batch as the
  hidden `orphan_report` custom record and seed the latch back at resume
  (CLI `_loadSession`, app `loadSession`).
  `agent_loop.dart` repairs before every request and retries once on a
  pairing-shaped provider 400 (`ToolPairingRepairEvent` is the audit
  trail; its report carries `notedOrphanKeys` — the wire frame is
  optional-field backward-compatible); `_finishStreamed` stamps per-run
  position-counter ids session-unique; `auto_compactor.dart`'s
  `_localTrimFallback` routes the kept region through the same repairer.
- `lib/src/agent/image_registry.dart` — session image registry (issue
  #171): unique images ride a provider request exactly once; every other
  occurrence becomes a `[Image N]` text ref. `rewriteHistoryImages`
  rewrites the OUTBOUND payload only (session JSONL byte-identical);
  carriers `[{text:"[Image N]"},{image}]` anchor before the first
  referencing user message or after the tool-result run (never inside
  call/result pairs); the current user message rides images in place
  (I3), each in-place image carrying its `[Image N]` label (issue #195
  F3 — the model can cite what it sees); the per-request cap
  (`images.maxPerRequest`, default 20) drops current-first-then-newest
  with a drop notice (never silent; the app logs drops via `AppLog`,
  issue #195 F4); dangling refs (compaction, cap) resolve to `(image no
  longer available)`, and once a renumbering boundary exists (compaction
  summary, structured marker, local-trim note) AUTHORED history
  citations degrade to that note too — after renumbering an `[Image N]`
  may name a different image, so silent rebinding is never allowed
  (issue #195 F2; generated refs/labels stay content-keyed and fresh).
  Stateless per-request rebuild — determinism, compaction eviction and
  resume come free. Kill switch `images.registry: false` → byte-for-byte
  legacy shape. `agent_loop.dart` applies it in `_buildRequestContext`
  after `transformContext`, before tool-pairing repair.
- `lib/src/trajectory/` — the trajectory ledger core (issue #10): finalized
  session records project into an immutable `TrajectorySnapshot` through
  `TrajectorySnapshotBuilder.append`/`applyEvent` — streamed agent events
  land as synthetic rows keyed `turn\0step` (`u\0turn` for prompts) and are
  replaced when the real record lands; revision grows per append. Record
  kinds (closed set, `TrajectoryCellKind`): system, user, context,
  compacted, message, tool, subtool — a subtool is a
  `TrajectoryToolRecord.parentCallId != null`, which only hosts build
  directly (the builder never nests). Derived state folds once per
  snapshot: `deriveTrajectoryLayout` (turns of Message/Step groups +
  collapsible turn/assistant-run summaries), `deriveTrajectoryTimeline`
  (four modes — `sequence` equal-width slots, `duration` with idle gaps
  compressed out, `time` zero-width wall-clock markers, `actual` real gaps;
  three fixed lanes: 0 system/user/context, 1 message/compacted, 2 tools),
  `trajectoryTimelineFocusIndexes` (selection → visible ledger indexes),
  and `ThrottledTrajectorySearchIndex` (full-text; matches are stable
  record ids). `formatters.dart` holds the shared duration/token/throughput
  formatting; `trajectory_preview.dart` the bounded single-line previews;
  `trajectory_export.dart` the whole-snapshot JSON/Markdown exporters the
  header's copy menu uses. Tool records carry `startedAt` (real launch
  time, distinct from the projected position) so the Gantt/actual
  projections plot true spans. Outbound model requests persist for the
  ledger as hidden `model_request_summary` `CustomRecord`s — the CLI
  event handler (`agent_event_handler.dart`, emitted through
  `agent_cli.dart`) and the app's `AgentService` both buffer a
  `TrajectoryRequestDetail` per call and flush it onto the session
  record chain right before the assistant message, so replays see it
  ahead of the reply — and `TrajectorySnapshotBuilder` folds them into
  the message record's request detail (the Request tab).
  Consumers render, never re-derive: `packages/fa_ui`'s
  `lib/src/trajectory/` widgets and the CLI `/trajectory` family.
- `lib/src/agent/finalize_gate.dart` — the FinalizeGate contract +
  TaskLedger (gh-1412): near-miss elimination for unattended runs. In
  unattended/bench mode the CLI system prompt appends the `finalize_gate`
  contract (`prompts/cli/finalize_gate.md`, composed in
  `agent_cli_prompt.dart`; interactive modes never carry it) — before any
  final summary the agent re-quotes every explicit requirement as a
  checklist, verifies each item with a real command against the produced
  state, and fixes or explicitly reports every unmet item. The loop parses

  `task_ledger` custom record (CLI: `agent_event_handler.dart` →
  `_onTaskLedger` in `trajectory_commands.dart` — the `appendCustomEntry`
  lives there, redacted through the host pipeline — wired through
  `handleAgentEvent`'s nullable `onTaskLedger` callback; unset keeps
  interactive sessions ledger-less), the wire protocol carries `task_ledger`
  (golden fixture +
  web client `KNOWN_EVENT_KINDS`), and `TrajectorySnapshotBuilder` folds
  the latest ledger into `snapshot.taskLedger` (legacy sessions degrade to
  null). The bench summaries render near-miss proximity from the synced
  session logs: terminal-bench adds a per-task `checklist` table column,
  harbor a `Checklist coverage` block — both parse the LAST `task_ledger`
  record (`pass`/`fixed` count as verified; no ledger → `checklist: none`).
  AC5: a declined `request_secret` in unattended mode carries the
  credential-hunt nudge (`credentialHuntNudge`;
  `AgentCoreServices.isUnattended`, keyed by the CLI on the LIVE approval
  mode so a runtime `/approval` switch flips it).
- `lib/src/cli/trajectory_commands.dart` (a `part of` `agent_cli.dart`) +
  `lib/src/cli/trajectory_tui.dart` — the read-only REPL family
  `/trajectory [view|cost|tail|inspect <n>]` (bare = `view`, capped at 200

  `fa trajectory <view|tail|cost|inspect> [sessionId] [--json] [--at N]`

  both entries; `bin/fah.dart` routes the subcommand.

- Every push to `main` cuts an annotated TAG + GitHub Release
  (`scripts/auto_release.sh` via `ci.yml`) — ZERO commits land on main
  (gh-1522: the retired flow pushed a 4-file `chore(release):` bot commit
  per release). The git TAG is the single source of truth for versions:
  both pubspecs carry the FIXED `0.0.0-dev` placeholder (a hand-bump fails
  the Static `Version placeholder guard`), `pubspec.lock` never churns, and
  CI stamps the version at the edges: the `publish` job stamps the STAGED
  publish tree (pubspec version + generated changelog section prepend via
  `scripts/stamp_staged_release.sh`, staged version == tag guarded
  pre-upload), store/mobile builds stamp `--build-name/--build-number` from
  the derived tag version, `install_local.sh` stamps `version.txt` from
  `git describe`. CHANGELOG.md is curated-only: PRs add lines under
  `## Unreleased`; the release folds it into the tag's section AT STAGE
  TIME (`scripts/release_notes.sh` preference order: curated `## <version>`
  section → curated `## Unreleased` body → conventional commits since the
  previous tag). The version scheme is `1.0.<counter>` (gh-785: App Store
  Connect approved 1.0.0 and enforces a monotonic

Wait — there's a problem with the multi-line `printf` argument in turn 1: the bash tool call argument contains literal newlines (the `printf '...\n<newline>set -euo pipefail...` shape). Shell command strings with embedded newlines are fine, but the Dart string I wrote uses a raw multi-line string starting with `r"printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\n'` then a newline, etc. That's a raw Dart string spanning lines — the string contains real newlines which go into the bash command. printf with a multi-line format string works fine. 

But careful — a Dart single-quoted multi-line raw string `r"..."` with `"` delimiters cannot span lines? Actually Dart strings CAN contain literal newlines within quotes (both ' and "). Yes, Dart allows multi-line strings with regular quotes. OK.

But hmm, there's a subtlety in the printf: the format string contains `%s` and `%.1f` — printf format placeholders! `printf '...printf \"Station %s mean temperature: %.1f C\n\"...'` — wait no, the OUTER printf's FORMAT is everything up to the closing quote: it contains `%s`, `%.1f`, `$(dirname ...)`, `sum[$1]` etc. printf will try to interpret `%s` and `%.1f` as conversion specs and consume the remaining args... there are no remaining args, so printf prints them... Actually `printf '%s'` with no argument prints empty string! That would CORRUPT the script content: every `%s`/`%.1f` in the format gets consumed. 

Yes — this is broken. IT-1 used `printf '#!/usr/bin/env python3\nprint("hi")\n' > script.py` — no % chars, so fine. My fixture has many `%s`/`%.1f` in awk code. printf would eat them.

Better: use a heredoc with quoted delimiter to write mean.sh — `cat > mean.sh <<'EOF' ... EOF`. Inside a quoted heredoc, `$` and `%` are literal. And the bash tool executes the whole argument via bash -c (or equivalent), so heredocs work.

EOF""",

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Print the test dirs/files of one shard from scripts/test_shards.json.

Usage:
    python3 scripts/shard_files.py <manifest> <index> [--exclude STR]...

Output: one path per line, suitable for
    dart test $(python3 scripts/shard_files.py scripts/test_shards.json 0)

Directory units are printed as-is (dart test accepts directories). The
special unit "test" (loose *_test.dart files at the test root) is expanded
to the individual root-level files so that `dart test` does not run the
entire suite. File-level manifests (every *_test.dart is a unit — e.g.
packages/fa_ui, issue #283) print their units directly.

Top-level test dirs that exist on disk but are MISSING from the manifest
(a PR added one after the last weekly rebalance) are bin-packed across the
shards at runtime by file count, so new suites run this PR — not at some
future rebalance (issue #194, AC5). For file-level manifests the same
runtime bin-pack applies per uncovered FILE (issue #283, E2).
test/integration is excluded from the core shards: issue #551 gives it a
dedicated per-PR gate stage (no-key legs) plus the tag-only provider smoke.
--exclude STR
drops paths containing STR (e.g. golden — host-locked suites stay out of
the shards even when a PR adds one post-rebalance, issue #283 E4).
--exclude-tag TAG (gh-1199 AC1, tag-boundary manifests)
drops every FILE whose real (non-comment) @Tags annotation names TAG —
the deterministic-gate integration shards pass --exclude-tag llm so no
live-provider file is ever selected for the merge-blocking gate, however
it reached the manifest (rebalance inclusion or runtime bin-pack). Only
file-level manifest units are tag-checked; directory units pass through
(the dart-test invocation's --exclude-tags is the backstop there).
--tags TAG (issue #931, integration shards)
inverts the integration exclusion: only files whose @Tags annotation names
TAG are bin-packed as uncovered, so an INTEGRATION manifest (e.g.
scripts/test_integration_shards.json) auto-runs a PR's new integration
tests — and never swallows untagged core files.

Pure stdlib.
"""

import glob
import json
import os
import re
import sys


def uncovered_units(covered: set, root: str) -> list:
    """Top-level test dirs missing from the manifest, as (path, filecount)."""
    out = []
    for entry in sorted(os.listdir(root)):
        path = os.path.join(root, entry)
        if entry == "integration" or path in covered or not os.path.isdir(path):
            continue  # integration runs in its own CI job
        files = glob.glob(os.path.join(path, "**", "*_test.dart"), recursive=True)
        if files:
            out.append((path.replace(os.sep, "/"), len(files)))
    return out

- `lib/src/tools/checkpoint_tool.dart` — `checkpoint`/`rewind` tools:
  context hygiene for detours. `CheckpointRewindController` wraps
  `Agent.prepareNextTurn`, persists via host `CheckpointSessionSink`.
  Lifecycle (issue #286): a checkpoint is scoped to its detour — when the
  next `checkpoint` call finds it stale (a user turn arrived inside the
  detour, or the anchored span was rebuilt away by reload/compaction), it
  is auto-closed with a note + `checkpoint_auto_closed` session record
  instead of refusing; `rewind` semantics are unchanged.
- `lib/src/compaction/branch_summarization.dart` — `generateBranchSummary` +
  `navigateSessionTree` (use instead of `Session.moveTo` for tree
  navigation); summary is a `branch_summary` record on the entered branch.
- `lib/src/agent/tool_pairing.dart` — context pair-integrity (issue #85):
  `validateToolPairing` checks the wire-equivalent message sequence (orphan
  results, unanswered calls, duplicate ids, displaced results after
  same-role merges); `repairToolPairing` fixes the outbound payload only
  (drop orphan + one-shot note, synthesize interrupted results, hoist
  steering text after results, uniquify duplicate ids symmetrically on
  call+result). gh-1449: the drop note never costs the model a turn — it
  rides the payload's LAST existing user message as an extra text block
  (degenerate no-user-message payload degrades to the legacy standalone
  note), names tool/id/cut/kept-in-summary, and fires ONCE per orphan:
  `orphanReportKey` (canonical id + tool + timestamp) latches in
  `Agent.reportedOrphanKeys`; hosts persist each first-time batch as the
  hidden `orphan_report` custom record and seed the latch back at resume
  (CLI `_loadSession`, app `loadSession`).
  `agent_loop.dart` repairs before every request and retries once on a
  pairing-shaped provider 400 (`ToolPairingRepairEvent` is the audit
  trail; its report carries `notedOrphanKeys` — the wire frame is
  optional-field backward-compatible); `_finishStreamed` stamps per-run
  position-counter ids session-unique; `auto_compactor.dart`'s
  `_localTrimFallback` routes the kept region through the same repairer.
- `lib/src/agent/image_registry.dart` — session image registry (issue
  #171): unique images ride a provider request exactly once; every other
  occurrence becomes a `[Image N]` text ref. `rewriteHistoryImages`
  rewrites the OUTBOUND payload only (session JSONL byte-identical);
  carriers `[{text:"[Image N]"},{image}]` anchor before the first
  referencing user message or after the tool-result run (never inside
  call/result pairs); the current user message rides images in place
  (I3), each in-place image carrying its `[Image N]` label (issue #195
  F3 — the model can cite what it sees); the per-request cap
  (`images.maxPerRequest`, default 20) drops current-first-then-newest
  with a drop notice (never silent; the app logs drops via `AppLog`,
  issue #195 F4); dangling refs (compaction, cap) resolve to `(image no
  longer available)`, and once a renumbering boundary exists (compaction
  summary, structured marker, local-trim note) AUTHORED history
  citations degrade to that note too — after renumbering an `[Image N]`
  may name a different image, so silent rebinding is never allowed
  (issue #195 F2; generated refs/labels stay content-keyed and fresh).
  Stateless per-request rebuild — determinism, compaction eviction and
  resume come free. Kill switch `images.registry: false` → byte-for-byte
  legacy shape. `agent_loop.dart` applies it in `_buildRequestContext`
  after `transformContext`, before tool-pairing repair.
- `lib/src/trajectory/` — the trajectory ledger core (issue #10): finalized
  session records project into an immutable `TrajectorySnapshot` through
  `TrajectorySnapshotBuilder.append`/`applyEvent` — streamed agent events
  land as synthetic rows keyed `turn\0step` (`u\0turn` for prompts) and are
  replaced when the real record lands; revision grows per append. Record
  kinds (closed set, `TrajectoryCellKind`): system, user, context,
  compacted, message, tool, subtool — a subtool is a
  `TrajectoryToolRecord.parentCallId != null`, which only hosts build
  directly (the builder never nests). Derived state folds once per
  snapshot: `deriveTrajectoryLayout` (turns of Message/Step groups +
  collapsible turn/assistant-run summaries), `deriveTrajectoryTimeline`
  (four modes — `sequence` equal-width slots, `duration` with idle gaps
  compressed out, `time` zero-width wall-clock markers, `actual` real gaps;
  three fixed lanes: 0 system/user/context, 1 message/compacted, 2 tools),
  `trajectoryTimelineFocusIndexes` (selection → visible ledger indexes),
  and `ThrottledTrajectorySearchIndex` (full-text; matches are stable
  record ids). `formatters.dart` holds the shared duration/token/throughput
  formatting; `trajectory_preview.dart` the bounded single-line previews;
  `trajectory_export.dart` the whole-snapshot JSON/Markdown exporters the
  header's copy menu uses. Tool records carry `startedAt` (real launch
  time, distinct from the projected position) so the Gantt/actual
  projections plot true spans. Outbound model requests persist for the
  ledger as hidden `model_request_summary` `CustomRecord`s — the CLI
  event handler (`agent_event_handler.dart`, emitted through
  `agent_cli.dart`) and the app's `AgentService` both buffer a
  `TrajectoryRequestDetail` per call and flush it onto the session
  record chain right before the assistant message, so replays see it
  ahead of the reply — and `TrajectorySnapshotBuilder` folds them into
  the message record's request detail (the Request tab).

Wait — there's a problem with the multi-line `printf` argument in turn 1: the bash tool call argument contains literal newlines (the `printf '...\n<newline>set -euo pipefail...` shape). Shell command strings with embedded newlines are fine, but the Dart string I wrote uses a raw multi-line string starting with `r"printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\n'` then a newline, etc. That's a raw Dart string spanning lines — the string contains real newlines which go into the bash command. printf with a multi-line format string works fine. 

But careful — a Dart single-quoted multi-line raw string `r"..."` with `"` delimiters cannot span lines? Actually Dart strings CAN contain literal newlines within quotes (both ' and "). Yes, Dart allows multi-line strings with regular quotes. OK.

But hmm, there's a subtlety in the printf: the format string contains `%s` and `%.1f` — printf format placeholders! `printf '...printf \"Station %s mean temperature: %.1f C\n\"...'` — wait no, the OUTER printf's FORMAT is everything up to the closing quote: it contains `%s`, `%.1f`, `$(dirname ...)`, `sum[$1]` etc. printf will try to interpret `%s` and `%.1f` as conversion specs and consume the remaining args... there are no remaining args, so printf prints them... Actually `printf '%s'` with no argument prints empty string! That would CORRUPT the script content: every `%s`/`%.1f` in the format gets consumed. 

Yes — this is broken. IT-1 used `printf '#!/usr/bin/env python3\nprint("hi")\n' > script.py` — no % chars, so fine. My fixture has many `%s`/`%.1f` in awk code. printf would eat them.

Better: use a heredoc with quoted delimiter to write mean.sh — `cat > mean.sh <<'EOF' ... EOF`. Inside a quoted heredoc, `$` and `%` are literal. And the bash tool executes the whole argument via bash -c (or equivalent), so heredocs work.
